nodes.title: Cloud fundamentals (CLF-C02 / AZ-900 / CCNA): Key Ideas
nodes.content: Cloud fundamentals questions appear on almost every entry-level certification. They test your ability to map a business requirement to the correct service model (IaaS/PaaS/SaaS), understand the provider vs customer responsibility split, and compare on-premises capex to cloud opex — all before any technical deep-dive.

flashcards.front: IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS — who manages what in each model?
flashcards.back: IaaS (EC2, Azure VM, Compute Engine): provider manages hardware + hypervisor; you manage OS, runtime, app, data. PaaS (App Service, Elastic Beanstalk, App Engine): provider adds OS + runtime; you manage app + data. SaaS (Office 365, Salesforce): provider manages everything; you manage user config and data. As you move up the stack you trade control for speed.

flashcards.front: Shared responsibility model — where is the exact dividing line?
flashcards.back: The provider is always responsible for security OF the cloud (physical data centers, networking fabric, hypervisor, managed service software). The customer is always responsible for security IN the cloud (data classification, IAM configuration, OS patching on IaaS VMs, application code). The dividing line shifts up the stack for PaaS and SaaS — the more managed the service, the more the provider owns.

flashcards.front: Regions vs Availability Zones — what is each?
flashcards.back: A region is a geographic cluster of data centers (e.g., us-east-1, West Europe). An AZ is one or more discrete data centers within a region with independent power, cooling, and networking. AZs in a region are close enough for low-latency synchronous replication but far enough apart that a fire/flood in one doesn't hit another. Spread workloads across at least 2 AZs for high availability.

flashcards.front: Capex vs opex — why does cloud shift the spending model?
flashcards.back: Capex (capital expenditure): large upfront purchase of hardware that you then depreciate over years; on-premises servers. Opex (operating expenditure): ongoing pay-as-you-go cost; cloud compute bills. Cloud converts infra from capex to opex — no hardware procurement lead times, costs scale with actual usage, easier to budget for a startup or to kill a failed project without a sunk-cost legacy.

nodes.title: What connects the LAN to the internet?

choices: Router
Network hub
Repeater
Wireless access point

nodes.explanation: A router forwards packets between networks (the LAN and the ISP/WAN) and is the default gateway out to the internet. A switch only moves frames within the LAN.

nodes.title: Security fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Security is about layering defenses so no single failure compromises a system. Most exams test the same core ideas: least privilege, defense in depth, the CIA triad, and the shared-responsibility line between you and your cloud provider.

flashcards.front: What is the CIA triad?
flashcards.back: Confidentiality (only the right people see the data), Integrity (data isn't tampered with), Availability (the system is reachable when needed). Every security control maps to at least one of these three pillars.

flashcards.front: What does 'least privilege' mean?
flashcards.back: Grant each identity (user, role, service account) the minimum permissions needed to do its job — no more. The opposite is wildcard access, which makes a single credential leak catastrophic.

flashcards.front: What is defense in depth?
flashcards.back: Stack multiple, independent controls so an attacker has to defeat all of them. Example: WAF in front of an app, network ACL on the subnet, IAM on the workload, encryption at rest in the database.

flashcards.front: Shared responsibility model — who does what?
flashcards.back: The cloud provider secures the cloud (physical hardware, hypervisor, region facilities). You secure what's IN the cloud (your data, IAM config, OS patching on EC2, application code). The exact line shifts by service: serverless is more on the provider, IaaS is more on you.

nodes.title: IP routing: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Routing is how packets find their way through a multi-network internet. Every router runs a forwarding table; routing protocols (OSPF, EIGRP, BGP) are the mechanisms by which routers exchange information and build that table.

flashcards.front: What's the longest-prefix-match rule?
flashcards.back: When multiple routes match a destination, the router picks the one with the most-specific (longest) prefix. So `10.0.0.0/24` beats `10.0.0.0/16` for a packet to `10.0.0.5`. This is how more-specific routes can override defaults.

flashcards.front: Default route — what does `0.0.0.0/0` mean?
flashcards.back: It matches every destination, so it's used only when no more-specific route exists. Typically points to the internet gateway. On a stub network, the default route is often the ONLY route — everything not local goes 'up' to a smarter router.

flashcards.front: Static vs dynamic routing — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Static routes are hand-configured, easy to understand, perfect for small or stub networks. Dynamic routing (OSPF, BGP, EIGRP) auto-discovers topology, reacts to link failures, scales to thousands of routers. Use dynamic the moment the topology is non-trivial or expected to change.

flashcards.front: Administrative distance — what is it?
flashcards.back: When the same destination is learned from multiple sources (static + OSPF + BGP), the router prefers the one with the lowest administrative distance. Defaults (Cisco): connected=0, static=1, EIGRP=90, OSPF=110, BGP=200. It's the tie-breaker before the routing-protocol metric.

questions.q: An IGP advertises ENTIRE routing table to neighbours every 30 seconds and uses HOP COUNT (max 15) as its metric. Loop-prevention is via split-horizon + route-poisoning. The algorithm behind it is Bellman-Ford. Which protocol fits this description?
choices: OSPF — link-state, Dijkstra/SPF, not Bellman-Ford
EIGRP — advanced distance-vector with DUAL, not Bellman-Ford
RIP
BGP — path-vector, uses best-path selection, not Bellman-Ford
questions.explanation: RIP (Routing Information Protocol) uses the Bellman-Ford algorithm and hop count as its metric. OSPF uses Dijkstra's SPF algorithm, EIGRP uses DUAL.

questions.q: A campus with mixed Cisco + HP + Juniper routers needs FIRST-HOP REDUNDANCY (default-gateway HA) using an OPEN-standard protocol that every vendor implements natively. The protocol elects a virtual IP and virtual MAC across two or more routers in active/standby. Which?
choices: VRRP
HSRP — Cisco proprietary, no Juniper/HP support
GLBP — Cisco proprietary with load balancing
EIGRP — routing protocol, not first-hop redundancy
questions.explanation: VRRP (Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol) is the IEEE standard for default gateway redundancy — vendor neutral. HSRP and GLBP are Cisco-proprietary. All use a virtual IP/MAC shared among routers.

questions.q: A distance-vector routing protocol prevents one specific loop pattern by REFUSING to advertise a route back out the interface from which the route was learned. The rule alone doesn't catch all loops but combined with route-poisoning and hold-down it covers most. What is this rule called?
choices: Splitting one broadcast domain into halves
Area route summarisation — OSPF / EIGRP feature, different
Update fragmentation
Split horizon
questions.explanation: Split horizon prevents routing loops by not advertising routes back the direction they came from. Split horizon with poison reverse sends the route back with infinite metric (poison) instead.

questions.q: Two large ISPs negotiate to exchange routes for hundreds of thousands of customer prefixes. The protocol carries an AS_PATH attribute, supports policy via communities + local-pref + MED, and is the only routing protocol that runs between distinct Autonomous Systems on the public internet. Which protocol?
choices: An IGP for flat sites
BGP
Cisco-proprietary protocol
Distance-vector by hop count
questions.explanation: BGP (EGP) manages routing between autonomous systems (AS numbers). It's used by ISPs to exchange routes on the internet and by enterprises with multiple ISP connections (multihoming). Path vector protocol.

questions.q: A Cisco ACL line uses `permit ip 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.255 any`. The second value is the wildcard mask. Wildcard 0 means 'must match', wildcard 1 means 'don't care'. For the /24 network 10.0.0.0/24, the wildcard mask written explicitly is 0.0.0.255 — the INVERSE bit pattern of 255.255.255.0. Which describes a wildcard mask?
choices: Inverse of a subnet mask — 0 bits MUST match, 1 bits are ignored (don't care)
Same as the subnet mask applied twice
An IPv6-only construct with no wildcard bits in IPv4 ACLs
Identical to CIDR notation; a /24 prefix has a wildcard of 255.255.255.0
questions.explanation: Wildcard masks are the bitwise inverse of subnet masks: subnet 255.255.255.0 → wildcard 0.0.0.255. Bits set to 0 must match the address exactly; bits set to 1 are wildcards. Used in IOS ACLs and OSPF network statements.

questions.q: An ISP wants to advertise ONE prefix that covers FOUR contiguous /24 customer networks (203.0.113.0/24, 203.0.114.0/24, 203.0.115.0/24, 203.0.116.0/24 — wait, only 113-116 are contiguous if aligned). Combining contiguous blocks into one larger prefix to shrink the routing table is called what?
choices: Supernetting / CIDR aggregation
Subnetting — splits a classful network into smaller pieces; the OPPOSITE direction
VXLAN stretched VLAN — L2 extension, different concept
Firewall rule grouping — security policy organisation, not routing aggregation
questions.explanation: Supernetting (route aggregation) advertises multiple contiguous networks as one summary route — reduces routing table size on internet-facing routers. ISPs aggregate customer prefixes; enterprises aggregate branch routes.

questions.q: Two OSPF routers on the same Ethernet broadcast segment exchange Hello packets to discover each other and verify the neighbour is still alive. Defaults: Hello every 10 s, Dead 4× the Hello (40 s). If either side has different timer values, no adjacency forms. What is the purpose of these timers?
choices: Hello = keepalive interval (10 s default)
Hello + Dead compute the route metric
Hello + Dead encrypt OSPF messages
Hello + Dead define OSPF areas
questions.explanation: OSPF Hello and Dead intervals must match between neighbors. Default: Hello=10s, Dead=40s on Ethernet. Mismatch = no adjacency. Lower timers = faster failure detection but more CPU/bandwidth. Never-match is a common misconfiguration.

questions.q: A branch router has specific routes for the local subnets and a CATCH-ALL route for anything else, pointing at the WAN edge: `ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 198.51.100.1`. Any packet that doesn't match a more specific entry follows this route. What is it called?
choices: OSPF `default-information originate` — propagates a default into OSPF, related but a different mechanism
Loopback /32 route — describes the router's local loopback, not the catch-all
Default route (0.0.0.0/0)
Static /32 host route — points at a single host, not a catch-all
questions.explanation: The default route (0.0.0.0/0) is the least specific route — matches everything. Routers apply longest prefix match: /32 > /24 > /16 > /0. The default route catches all traffic with no more-specific match and forwards it upstream.

nodes.title: Order the OSI model layers

data.scenario: Arrange the seven OSI layers from Layer 1 (bottom) up to Layer 7 (top).

nodes.explanation: The OSI model runs Layer 1 Physical, 2 Data Link, 3 Network, 4 Transport, 5 Session, 6 Presentation, 7 Application. Mnemonic (bottom-up): Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away.

nodes.title: Network operations (CompTIA Network+): Key Ideas
nodes.content: Network+ tests operational fundamentals: how SNMP works for device monitoring, why baseline documentation matters, the change-management process that prevents accidental outages, and syslog severity levels that tell you how serious a message is. These appear in scenario questions where you're asked which tool to use or which process was skipped.

flashcards.front: SNMP — OID, MIB, community string, v2c vs v3.
flashcards.back: OID (Object Identifier): a dotted-number path in the MIB tree that uniquely identifies one piece of device data (e.g., `1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.10` = ifInOctets). MIB (Management Information Base): the schema/dictionary that maps OIDs to human-readable names. Community string: a plain-text password used for SNMP v1/v2c authentication — typically 'public' (read) and 'private' (write); a well-known security weakness. SNMPv3 replaces community strings with proper user-based auth (MD5/SHA) and encryption (AES/DES).

flashcards.front: Why is network baseline documentation critical?
flashcards.back: A baseline records normal traffic volumes, CPU/memory levels, error rates, and routing tables — captured during a known-good period. When something goes wrong, you compare current readings to the baseline to spot the anomaly (utilization spiked 300%, a new route appeared, error rate tripled). Without a baseline, 'high CPU' is meaningless because you don't know what 'normal' was. Network+ expects you to identify baselining as a best practice before troubleshooting.

flashcards.front: Change management process — what are the key steps?
flashcards.back: Request change → assess risk and impact → obtain approval (CAB or manager) → schedule a maintenance window → implement → test and verify → document outcome → close. The exam distinguishes emergency changes (faster approval path for critical incidents) from standard changes (pre-approved, low-risk, routine). Skipping change management is the most common cause of self-inflicted outages.

flashcards.front: Syslog severity levels 0–7 — name them.
flashcards.back: 0 Emergency, 1 Alert, 2 Critical, 3 Error, 4 Warning, 5 Notice, 6 Informational, 7 Debug. Lower number = more severe. Most organizations alert on 0–3 and log 0–6. Debug (7) produces enormous volume and is usually enabled only during active troubleshooting. The mnemonic: Every Awful Crisis Erodes Wisdom, No Debate.

questions.q: A network monitoring system polls routers, switches, and firewalls every 60 s for interface byte counters, CPU, memory, environment sensors. It can also SET variables (with the right community / user). Communication is UDP 161 (polls) / UDP 162 (traps). Which protocol?
choices: A VPN tunnel protocol
SNMP
SSH — remote-shell protocol, not bulk metric polling
RIP — distance-vector routing protocol, not management
questions.explanation: SNMP (v1, v2c, v3) lets a Network Management System poll device counters (CPU, interfaces, errors) and push configuration. Always prefer SNMPv3 — it adds authentication and encryption to the management plane.

questions.q: Before going live, an ops team measures over two weeks the normal range of: per-link utilisation, latency between key endpoints, error counters, and application response time. They store this as a reference. Months later they compare CURRENT measurements against the reference to detect deviation. What's this reference called?
choices: Network baseline
SLA floor — the contractual minimum, not the measured normal
Default vendor configuration — what's shipped, not what's measured
Factory-reset template — bootstrap config, not performance
questions.explanation: A baseline captures normal performance (bandwidth utilization, latency, error rates, CPU). When issues arise, comparing current metrics against the baseline quickly identifies anomalies.

questions.q: An NOC team is documenting their environment for a new on-call engineer. They produce a diagram showing routers, switches, firewalls, links, port assignments, and IP / VLAN labels — both physical patching AND logical L3 paths. What is this artefact called?
choices: Application architecture diagram — software tiers, not network devices
HR organisation chart — people hierarchy, unrelated
Directory hierarchy diagram — AD users / OUs, unrelated
Network topology diagram
questions.explanation: Physical topology: actual cable/device layout. Logical topology: how data flows. Network diagrams help technicians understand the network, troubleshoot faster, and plan changes without disruption.

questions.q: An enterprise wants ONE central system for: (a) IPv4/IPv6 address space planning + allocation, (b) DHCP scope management, (c) DNS zone management, (d) per-IP audit trail. Vendors include Infoblox, BlueCat, Solarwinds. What's this category of system?
choices: Network-monitoring system — polls SNMP counters for performance management; does not manage IP address space, DHCP scopes, or provide a per-IP audit trail
IP Address Management (IPAM) — manages IP space + DHCP + DNS + audit centrally
Network Access Control — provides device posture management and quarantine; does not manage IP address allocation, DHCP, or DNS zone administration
A link-state routing protocol — provides topology management and IP reachability for routers; not a system for tracking IP address space or managing DHCP/DNS services
questions.explanation: IPAM tools (Windows Server IPAM, phpIPAM, Infoblox) provide visibility into IP address utilization, prevent conflicts, manage DHCP scopes, and integrate with DNS. Critical for large networks to avoid IP chaos.

questions.q: A network operator needs to manage routers and switches even when the data network is DOWN (firmware push, recovery, config rollback). A separate physical path via console servers + dedicated mgmt NICs sits on a completely separate set of cables. What's this management path called?
choices: Out-of-band management
Reused corporate internet via VPN
VLAN 1 as management VLAN — in-band, fails with the data plane
Wireless backup network — in-band, depends on the data network
questions.explanation: OOB management uses separate physical connectivity (dedicated management ports, cellular modems, console servers). Critical for restoring failed devices when production network is unavailable.

questions.q: An NOC routes log events from routers, switches, firewalls, and Linux servers to a central log server using UDP/TCP 514. Each event carries a severity code 0-7. Which describes the system + the severity scale?
choices: Central syslog server
Application performance monitor (APM) — traces transaction response times and user experience metrics; not a central log aggregation server using syslog protocol
SNMP manager polling counters — queries MIBs via UDP 161 to collect interface and resource statistics; not a central syslog server receiving event streams on UDP/TCP 514
Firewall-only log aggregator — a device-specific log store; a central syslog server receives events from routers, switches, firewalls, and Linux servers simultaneously
questions.explanation: Syslog (UDP 514, TCP 6514 for TLS) forwards device logs to a central server. Common mnemonic: Every Awful Crisis Eventually Will Neglect Innocent Demons. Level 3 and above warrant immediate investigation.

questions.q: A network team produces TWO complementary diagrams for an audit: (1) LOGICAL — IP / VLAN / routing relationships, ignoring physical placement. (2) PHYSICAL — device location, rack-units, cable patching, IDF/MDF wiring. Which describes the two diagram types?
choices: Only the physical diagram matters for audits
Network diagrams are only useful during outages
Logical: IPs, VLANs, routing
Diagrams are unnecessary for small networks
questions.explanation: Good network documentation combines a logical diagram (IP addressing, VLAN map, routing) with a physical diagram (device locations, cable runs, rack layout). Both are essential for planning, change management, and rapid troubleshooting.

questions.q: An NTP client queries a peer that lists itself as Stratum 2 in its packets. The peer is two hops away (in NTP terms) from a primary reference clock (Stratum 1, e.g. a GPS-synced atomic clock = Stratum 0). What does the stratum number represent?
choices: Hop-distance from a Stratum 0 reference clock
An authentication strength tier indicating how many factors the NTP clock source requires
The NTP software version running on the queried time server
A key-authentication level controlling which NTP peers are trusted
questions.explanation: NTP stratum is the distance, in hops, from a Stratum-0 reference clock such as a GPS or atomic source. Stratum 1 servers are directly attached to that reference; Stratum 2 syncs from Stratum 1, and so on. Stratum 16 means unsynchronised.

nodes.title: Physical cabling (CompTIA Network+): Key Ideas
nodes.content: Network+ tests physical layer specifics: cable categories and their real-world speed/distance limits, the TIA-568-B wiring standard, PoE classes for powering devices over Ethernet, and common fault types like crosstalk and split pairs. These appear in both knowledge questions and troubleshooting scenarios.

flashcards.front: Cat6 vs Cat6a — what changes in speed and distance?
flashcards.back: Cat6: supports 1 Gbps (1000BASE-T) to 100 m and 10 Gbps (10GBASE-T) only to 55 m due to alien crosstalk. Cat6a ('augmented'): supports 10 Gbps to the full 100 m run by using a larger diameter and better shielding to control alien crosstalk. Use Cat6 for standard gigabit runs; use Cat6a for new 10G runs or when you want 10G path length flexibility.

flashcards.front: TIA-568-B pin-out — which wires go on which pins?
flashcards.back: 568-B (the most common standard): 1=white-orange, 2=orange, 3=white-green, 4=blue, 5=white-blue, 6=green, 7=white-brown, 8=brown. Pairs are 1-2 (orange), 3-6 (green), 4-5 (blue), 7-8 (brown). A crossover cable uses 568-B on one end and 568-A on the other, swapping pairs 1-2 and 3-6. Modern switches with Auto-MDIX detect and compensate for crossover automatically.

flashcards.front: PoE standards — what wattage does each provide?
flashcards.back: IEEE 802.3af (PoE): 15.4 W at the port, 12.95 W delivered to the device — covers IP phones, basic APs. 802.3at (PoE+): 30 W at port, 25.5 W delivered — PTZ cameras, dual-radio APs. 802.3bt (PoE++): Type 3 = 60 W; Type 4 = 90–100 W — high-power APs, video conferencing systems, thin clients. The powered device (PD) negotiates the class; the switch PSE must have sufficient total budget.

flashcards.front: Split pair vs crosstalk — what causes each and how do you detect them?
flashcards.back: Split pair: a wiring error where a twisted pair is broken up across two different pairs (e.g., pins 1 and 3 are paired instead of 1 and 2). The cable passes a continuity test but fails NEXT (near-end crosstalk) because the wire pairs no longer benefit from differential signaling. Crosstalk (NEXT/FEXT): electromagnetic coupling between pairs in a cable — caused by poor termination, untwisting too much at the connector, or using the wrong category cable. A cable tester with NEXT measurement catches both.

questions.q: A cable certifier reports `Split Pair` on a Cat6 patch cable. The fault is when wires from DIFFERENT twisted pairs (e.g., pair 1 white/blue and pair 2 white/orange) are swapped at the RJ-45 termination. Continuity passes end-to-end (1↔1, 2↔2, …) but crosstalk is terrible. What is the fault?
choices: Cable length exceeds 100 m — a different fault class reported as attenuation, not as a split pair wiring error
Both ends terminated to T568B — correct and matching termination; not a split pair or wiring fault
Damaged shielding — a physical fault causing EMI susceptibility but not a split pair wiring error
Split Pair
questions.explanation: A split pair occurs when wires from different twisted pairs are crossed at termination. The cable still passes basic continuity tests but suffers heavy near-end crosstalk, causing intermittent throughput and CRC errors.

questions.q: An installer is running Cat6 UTP from the IDF to user desks. The Ethernet standard caps the run length so end-to-end signal integrity stays within spec at 1 Gbps / 10 Gbps. What is the MAXIMUM end-to-end cable length for Cat5e/Cat6 UTP Ethernet?
choices: 500 m — far above the spec; signal would degrade well before
100 m total (90 m horizontal + 10 m patch cords)
questions.explanation: The maximum segment length for 10BASE-T, 100BASE-TX, and 1000BASE-T over UTP (Cat5e/Cat6) is 100 meters (328 feet), including patch cables.

questions.q: An IP phone or wireless AP attached to a single Cat6 cable receives BOTH its Ethernet data AND its DC power over the same 4-pair cable from the switch port. The switch port (PSE) detects the device (PD), classifies its power class, and supplies up to 90 W (802.3bt). What is this technology called?
choices: Power over Ethernet (PoE / 802.3af / at / bt)
Field cable certification — testing equipment specification, not power delivery
5-GHz wireless — wireless transmission, unrelated to wired PoE
100-Gbps Ethernet — high-speed standard, unrelated to PoE
questions.explanation: PoE (802.3af: 15.4W), PoE+ (802.3at: 30W), and PoE++ (802.3bt: 60-100W) power IP phones, wireless APs, IP cameras, and IoT devices through the network cable — no separate power outlet needed.

questions.q: A long inter-building data run is over 1 km. Copper UTP can't reach. The chosen medium uses LIGHT PULSES on glass strands, immune to EMI, and supports multi-km lengths at 10/40/100 Gbps with the right transceivers. What is it?
choices: Coax — copper conductor with shielding, no light pulses, ≤ 500 m on legacy 10BASE5
Copper with fibre-mesh insulation
Wireless point-to-point — useful but susceptible to weather/LoS
Fibre optic
questions.explanation: Fiber optic cabling is immune to electromagnetic interference, carries far more bandwidth than copper, reaches much greater distances (single-mode up to ~80 km, multi-mode up to ~2 km), and emits no electrical signal that can be tapped passively.

questions.q: An optical engineer compares two fibre flavours: (A) tiny ~9 µm core, ONE light path, used for inter-DC and metro links up to tens of km. (B) larger ~50-62.5 µm core, MULTIPLE light paths with modal dispersion, used for intra-DC under ~500 m at 10 Gbps. Which mapping?
choices: Multi-mode fiber is always faster than single-mode
Single-mode: one light path, longer reach (km)
Only multi-mode fiber supports Ethernet standards
Single-mode fiber is used for short runs under 100 m because its narrow core limits the light path
questions.explanation: Single-mode fiber has an 8-10 µm core, uses a laser source, and supports long reach (km). Multi-mode has a 50/62.5 µm core, uses LED/VCSEL sources, and is limited to roughly 2 km because modal dispersion broadens the pulse over distance.

questions.q: An installer terminating RJ-45 jacks must choose a pinout. The two standardised orderings are T568A and T568B. A STRAIGHT-THROUGH patch cable uses the SAME standard on both ends; a CROSSOVER cable uses ONE end with each standard (one T568A, the other T568B). Which statement is correct?
choices: T568A and T568B are TIA/EIA pinouts for RJ-45
T568B gives higher throughput on Cat 6
T568A is for fibre connectors
T568A is Cat5e and T568B is Cat6
questions.explanation: Both 568A and 568B are valid. Organizations standardize on one (most use 568B). Straight-through: same standard both ends — connects PC to switch. Crossover: 568A one end, 568B the other — connects PC to PC or switch to switch (modern NICs auto-MDIX makes crossovers unnecessary).

questions.q: An IP phone vendor's datasheet lists PoE classes: 802.3af up to 15.4 W per port, 802.3at up to 30 W, 802.3bt up to 60 / 90 W per port (Type 3 / 4). What family of IEEE standards does this describe?
choices: Ethernet speed standards (10/100/1000/10G)
VLAN-tagging extensions (802.1Q / ad)
Wireless enterprise auth
questions.explanation: PoE standards deliver power and data over Ethernet. 802.3af: basic PoE for IP phones, small APs. 802.3at: PoE+ for PTZ cameras, tablets. 802.3bt: PoE++ for laptops, multi-radio APs, smart lighting systems.

nodes.title: VLANs: Key Ideas
nodes.content: A VLAN logically segments a single physical switch into multiple broadcast domains. VLAN 10 traffic can't see VLAN 20 traffic without a Layer-3 routed hop, even on the same switch. This is the foundation of multi-tenant networking on shared hardware.

flashcards.front: Access port vs trunk port — what's the difference?
flashcards.back: An access port belongs to exactly one VLAN and strips the tag — end hosts don't see VLAN headers. A trunk port carries multiple VLANs between switches using 802.1Q tags. Hosts plug into access ports; switches connect to each other via trunks.

flashcards.front: What is the native VLAN on a trunk?
flashcards.back: The native VLAN is the one VLAN that's NOT tagged on a trunk — frames in that VLAN traverse the link with no 802.1Q header. Defaults to VLAN 1 but should be changed to an unused VLAN on every trunk for security (prevents VLAN hopping attacks).

flashcards.front: Why use a Layer-3 SVI?
flashcards.back: A Switched Virtual Interface (SVI) gives a VLAN a Layer-3 address inside the switch — it's the inter-VLAN router. Without an SVI (or external router), VLANs can't talk to each other. Modern switches do inter-VLAN routing in hardware at wire speed.

flashcards.front: What's VLAN hopping?
flashcards.back: An attacker tricks the switch into forwarding their traffic into a VLAN they shouldn't be in. Two flavors: double-tagging (exploits the native-VLAN-untagged rule) and switch-spoofing (the host negotiates a trunk via DTP). Mitigation: tag the native VLAN, set ports to access mode explicitly, disable DTP.

questions.q: An enterprise has one physical switch carrying traffic for SALES, FINANCE, and ENGINEERING. Each team's broadcast traffic should be isolated; finance frames must NOT leak to sales or engineering ports. A switch feature partitions the broadcast domain logically. What is this feature?
choices: Virtual Link between two remote offices
Variable Length Address Network
Virtual LAN (VLAN)
Very Large Area Network
questions.explanation: VLANs logically segment a single physical switch into multiple broadcast domains, improving security, performance, and network management without requiring separate hardware.

questions.q: An 802.1Q trunk carries VLAN 10, 20, 30 with `switchport trunk native vlan 99` set. A frame arrives on the trunk WITHOUT an 802.1Q tag. Which VLAN does the switch assign to that untagged frame, and what's the requirement for the configuration?
choices: The management VLAN — separate role; native VLAN is its own concept
Always VLAN 1
Highest-utilised VLAN on the trunk
The configured native VLAN (here 99)
questions.explanation: The native VLAN on a trunk receives untagged frames. Default is VLAN 1 on Cisco. If the native VLAN differs on each end of a trunk, traffic can hop VLANs (native VLAN mismatch attack vector).

questions.q: An L2 segment with multiple redundant inter-switch links must avoid endless frame circulation. Without intervention a broadcast frame would be flooded forever, multiplying at each switch. A protocol elects a root, calculates least-cost paths, and BLOCKS the redundant ports — preserving a loop-free active topology. Which?
choices: A BGP routing loop
A DNS resolution loop
L2 loop
BGP AS_PATH loop detection — L3 inter-AS, not L2 broadcast loops
questions.explanation: Layer 2 loops: frames have no TTL (unlike IP), so looping frames multiply exponentially causing broadcast storms. STP (802.1D) selects a root bridge and blocks redundant paths, creating a loop-free tree topology.

questions.q: A flat L2 segment with multiple inter-switch links AND no STP suddenly sees traffic on every port spiking to 100% utilisation. Every broadcast loops forever, multiplying in volume. Ping packets reach 100% loss. What's happening?
choices: Unusual unicast traffic spike from a single host — would not cause broadcasts to multiply and flood every port across multiple switches
A network loop is multiplying broadcasts/floods exponentially because STP is missing or broken
Volumetric DDoS attack from an external source — would create directional congestion on the uplink but would not cause L2 broadcasts to loop and multiply exponentially
IPTV multicast spike — typically contained by IGMP snooping on switches; would not produce the looping, multiplying broadcast storm pattern seen when STP is absent
questions.explanation: Broadcast storms occur when Ethernet frames loop between switches. Without STP, a single loop causes exponential frame multiplication. Symptoms: 100% link utilization, switch CPU at max, network unresponsive. STP prevents this.

questions.q: A service-provider backbone needs to carry the customer's 802.1Q-tagged VLANs across the SP core WITHOUT renumbering them. The SP wraps the customer frame in a SECOND 802.1Q tag (the S-Tag) before transmitting on the SP core; pops it on egress. What is this technology called?
choices: 802.1X — port-based network access control for authenticating devices on a LAN; a different IEEE standard, not a provider VLAN encapsulation technique
802.1ad / Q-in-Q (provider bridging)
IPsec double-encryption mode — encrypts data twice using nested security associations; a security mechanism unrelated to provider VLAN stacking
First-hop redundancy protocol (HSRP or VRRP) — provides gateway failover for end hosts; a different concept unrelated to provider VLAN transport
questions.explanation: QinQ encapsulates customer 802.1Q frames inside a provider S-Tag (outer VLAN). Customer can use any VLAN IDs (1-4094) — the provider only sees the outer S-Tag. Common in metro Ethernet and ISP aggregation networks.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.

questions.q: A wireless engineer is replacing a legacy 802.11g network. The replacement standard must support DUAL-BAND operation (both the original 2.4 GHz channel space AND the newer 5 GHz space) and offer MIMO. Which IEEE 802.11 amendment was the FIRST to operate on BOTH 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz?
choices: 802.11a — 5 GHz only
802.11g — 2.4 GHz only
802.11b — 2.4 GHz only
questions.explanation: 802.11n (Wi-Fi 4) operates on both 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz. 802.11a and 802.11ac use 5 GHz only. 802.11b and 802.11g use 2.4 GHz only.

questions.q: A wireless designer walks a building with a spectrum analyser + heatmap tool to determine: best AP locations, channel plan to minimise CCI, required AP density for target client SNR. Output is a deployment plan + RF heat map. What is this activity called?
choices: Site survey
Throughput speed test — post-deployment performance check, different activity
External security audit — policy/process, not RF
Inventory documentation — recording existing gear, not design
questions.explanation: Wireless site surveys (passive: listen, active: connect, predictive: software model) determine AP placement, channel assignments, power levels, and identify interference sources (microwaves, adjacent networks) before deployment.

questions.q: A wireless engineer is upgrading APs from Wi-Fi 5 (802.11ac) to a newer standard. The newer standard is dual-band (2.4 + 5 GHz), uses OFDMA to schedule multiple clients within one channel time-slot, MU-MIMO uplink + downlink, BSS Coloring to reduce co-channel interference, and Target Wake Time for IoT battery life. Which standard?
choices: 802.11n — older Wi-Fi 4, no OFDMA or BSS Coloring
Enterprise-only standard — licensing isn't gated this way
Wi-Fi 6 is 5-GHz-only
questions.explanation: Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) improvements: OFDMA (divide channels for multiple users simultaneously), MU-MIMO 8x8, BSS Coloring (reduces interference), TWT (Target Wake Time for IoT battery life). Wi-Fi 6E adds 6 GHz band.

questions.q: An IPv6 host comes up on a fresh interface. Even with NO RA / DHCPv6 received, it immediately has a usable address with prefix FE80::/10 that is scoped to ONE link — never routed off-segment. Which address category is this?
choices: Unique Local — FC00::/7, routable within an org (organisation-scoped)
Multicast — FF::/8, not the link-local
Global Unicast — 2000::/3, globally routable, opposite scope
Link-Local
questions.explanation: Link-local addresses (FE80::/10) are automatically assigned to every IPv6 interface and are only valid on the local link. They are never routed beyond the local segment.

questions.q: A network engineer enables IPv6 on a LAN. Hosts must auto-configure their own addresses from the router's advertised /64 prefix without requiring a stateful server to assign them. Which mechanism accomplishes this?
choices: Static manual addressing using EUI-64 host suffixes — requires an administrator to configure each host address manually; not an automatic mechanism driven by router advertisements
SLAAC with Router Advertisements from the gateway
DHCPv6 stateful mode with a managed address pool — uses a dedicated DHCPv6 server to assign addresses; not a stateless mechanism built from the router-advertised prefix
NAT64/DNS64 translation gateway — enables IPv6-only hosts to reach IPv4 destinations; not a mechanism for hosts to auto-configure addresses from router-advertised prefixes
questions.explanation: SLAAC (Stateless Address Autoconfiguration) lets hosts build their own IPv6 address from the /64 prefix in a Router Advertisement (RA) plus an interface identifier. DHCPv6 stateful mode requires a server to track and assign addresses.

questions.q: A service-provider backbone forwards customer packets using a SHORT (20-bit) label stack pushed onto each packet at the ingress PE, swapped at every P-router, and popped at the egress PE. No IP routing lookup happens inside the core — only label-based forwarding. Which technology?
choices: A BGP extension used in SP backbones that forwards packets using community attributes without requiring a label lookup
Wireless WPA3 encryption applied in backbone core segments so that forwarding decisions are encrypted
MPLS — Multiprotocol Label Switching; forwards by short labels, no IP-lookup in the core
A DSCP QoS marking scheme applied in the core that forwards short-priority packets on faster paths
questions.explanation: MPLS assigns short labels to packets at ingress. Core routers forward based on labels (not IP lookups) — much faster. Widely used by ISPs for VPNs, Traffic Engineering, and connecting enterprise sites.

questions.q: Two routers terminate a GRE tunnel for non-IP-encapsulated traffic. The underlying transport has no inherent reachability detection — so a one-way break leaves the tunnel 'up' even though traffic is black-holed. A feature periodically probes the remote end and brings the tunnel interface down if probes fail. Which feature?
choices: GRE signature authentication
IPComp compression
IPsec transport-mode wrapping
GRE keepalive
questions.explanation: GRE keepalives detect when the remote tunnel endpoint is unreachable (even if the physical interface is up). Without keepalives, the tunnel interface stays up and routing protocols don't detect the failure. Configured with 'tunnel keepalive'.

questions.q: An A record for `web.example.com → 203.0.113.42` is returned to a recursive resolver. The resolver CACHES the answer for a duration encoded in the response, then re-queries the authoritative when that timer expires. What's this caching timer called?
choices: Maximum DNS response wait time — the resolver timeout before retrying or failing; not the duration that a cached record remains valid
DNS TTL (Time To Live) — how long a record may be cached before re-resolution
DHCP server lease duration — the time a client may use a DHCP-assigned IP address; unrelated to DNS record caching
Maximum recursive hop count — the number of referral steps a recursive resolver may follow before returning SERVFAIL; not the caching duration of a record
questions.explanation: DNS TTL controls caching duration. Low TTL (300s) = faster DNS changes propagate but more queries to your DNS server. High TTL (86400s = 24h) = efficient caching but slower change propagation.
